passage: Blue paint was dripping off the art table in the kindergarten room. "Who spilled this?" asked Rashmi, the teacher. Jaya, five, hid her blue fingers behind her back. "Not me." Rashmi said nothing, but later, when Jaya said a classmate had pushed her in the line, Rashmi went to check with the others first. Jaya's cheeks burned. At home time she tugged Rashmi's sleeve. "The paint was me. Sorry." Rashmi knelt. "Thank you for telling me. That helps me believe you."

qa.q: Where was the blue paint dripping?
qa.a: It was dripping off the art table in the kindergarten room.

qa.q: Why did Jaya's cheeks burn when Rashmi checked with the others?
qa.a: She seemed to realise that her earlier lie was why Rashmi didn't simply believe her, and she felt embarrassed.

qa.q: Which choice by Rashmi helped Jaya learn about honesty?
qa.a: She thanked Jaya for telling the truth and explained that it helps her believe her, linking honesty to trust.

qa.q: How might the classmates see Jaya after the paint lie?
qa.a: They might trust her a little less at first, but her coming clean can help rebuild it.

grounding: It shows a child experimenting with a lie, seeing trust weaken, and then telling the truth.

passage: I'm Elizabeth, and my little sister Neelam is five. On Sunday Mummy asked who ate the last laddoo, and Neelam said, "Not me," with crumbs on her chin. Mummy found the paper under her pillow. On Tuesday Neelam said her tummy hurt, and Mummy asked, "Is that true, or is it like the laddoo?" Neelam looked shocked and started to cry. I'm not sure she understood why at first. That night she told Mummy, "I'll only say true things now."

qa.q: Where did Mummy find the laddoo paper?
qa.a: She found it under Neelam's pillow.

qa.q: Why might Neelam have looked shocked on Tuesday?
qa.a: She may have been hurt and surprised that Mummy doubted her, not expecting the laddoo lie to matter later.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Neelam understand trust after this?
qa.a: She could explain gently that true words help people believe us, and praise Neelam when she tells the truth.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Neelam's reaction?
qa.a: Elizabeth is not sure Neelam understood at first why Mummy doubted her, but notices her promise that night.

grounding: An older sister observes a child whose lie leads to her being doubted later.

passage:
Monday: "Did you brush?" Ramesh asked. "Yes," said Bhupen, though his toothbrush was dry. Ramesh touched it and raised an eyebrow.
Wednesday: Bhupen said he had put his toys away. Ramesh checked the room first. Bhupen pouted. "Why don't you believe me?"
"Remember the toothbrush?" Ramesh asked.
Saturday: A cup crashed in the kitchen. Bhupen came out, shoulders stiff. "I broke it, Papa. By mistake." Ramesh hugged him. "Thank you for the truth."

qa.q: How did Ramesh know Bhupen hadn't brushed?
qa.a: He touched the toothbrush and it was dry.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's pout on Wednesday show he was feeling?
qa.a: It shows he felt hurt and annoyed that his father didn't believe him.

qa.q: What helped Bhupen choose honesty on Saturday?
qa.a: Feeling what it was like to be doubted, and his father's calm reminder, helped him see that the truth keeps trust.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel when Bhupen admits breaking the cup?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and proud that Bhupen told the truth even when he was scared. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child's lie leading to lost trust over several days, then a truthful admission.

passage:
The lights went out just as Deepak, five, knocked Mummy's clay diya off the shelf. Crack.

When the torch came on, Mummy saw the pieces. "Who did this?"

"Siddharth did," Deepak said quickly. His little brother, only three, started to cry.

Mummy looked at Deepak for a long time. Next day, when Deepak said he'd finished his milk, she checked the glass. "Yesterday you told me something untrue," she said quietly. "Now it's hard to know when to believe you."

Deepak's ears burned. "I broke the diya," he whispered. "Sorry, Siddharth."

qa.q: What did Deepak knock off the shelf?
qa.a: He knocked Mummy's clay diya off the shelf, and it cracked.

qa.q: Why did Deepak's ears burn when Mummy checked his glass?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, realising his lie about the diya had made Mummy doubt him.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Deepak understand lying?
qa.a: She calmly showed him the result, that it became hard to believe him, instead of only punishing him.

qa.q: How was Siddharth affected by Deepak's lie?
qa.a: He was blamed for something he didn't do and started to cry, so the lie hurt him directly.

grounding: Shows a young child lying during a power cut, seeing trust break, and then telling the truth.

passage:
"Did you brush your teeth, Zeenat?" Abbu called from the kitchen of their Hyderabad flat.

"Yes!" Zeenat, five, said, still playing with her dolls.

Her older brother Tanvir came out of the bathroom holding her dry toothbrush. "It's not even wet."

Abbu raised his eyebrows. Zeenat looked at the floor.

That evening she said her tummy hurt. Abbu frowned. "Is that true, or like the toothbrush?"

"True!" she said, eyes filling. Abbu hugged her and checked. "Okay. But see how the toothbrush made it hard?"

qa.q: What did Tanvir bring out of the bathroom?
qa.a: He brought out Zeenat's dry toothbrush.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Abbu asked if her tummy ache was true?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, with eyes filling, because she was telling the truth and wasn't believed at first.

qa.q: How could Abbu help Zeenat learn from this without shaming her?
qa.a: He can keep gently linking the small lie to the trust problem, as he did, while still comforting and checking on her.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see his sister's lie?
qa.a: He seems a little pleased to catch her, but he may also learn that small lies make it harder for the family to trust each other.

grounding: Shows a young child discovering that a small lie makes others doubt her later.

passage:
“Kunal, why is the remote in two pieces?”
Kunal, five, looked at the floor. “The cat did it.”
Yogesh raised his eyebrows. “Kunal. We don't have a cat.”
Kunal's cheeks went pink. He twisted his T-shirt. “Maybe a cat came in the window.”
“Beta, if you tell me what really happened, I won't be angry.”
A long pause. “I was jumping on the sofa. It fell.”
Yogesh knelt down. “Thank you for telling me the truth. Now I know I can believe you. Let's fix it together.”

qa.q: What did Kunal first say broke the remote?
qa.a: He said the cat did it.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when his father said they don't have a cat?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and nervous, with pink cheeks, twisting his T-shirt.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh's response a good one?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked Kunal for the truth and explained that it helps him believe Kunal, so honesty felt safe.

qa.q: What would change if Yogesh had shouted as soon as Kunal lied?
qa.a: Kunal might have kept lying out of fear instead of learning that telling the truth builds trust.

grounding: A five-year-old tries a lie, is gently caught, and learns that truth keeps trust.

passage:
Class note, Thursday. Teacher: Charu.
On Monday, Tarun (five) told me he had finished his milk. Later I found the full cup behind the plant pot. I told him I felt sad that he didn't tell me the truth.
Today, Tarun said he had washed his hands, and his friend Veer said, “No, you didn't, you lie.” Tarun's face crumpled and he cried, “I did!” His hands were wet. He had.
Next step: we talked at circle time about how lies make it hard for people to believe us, even when we're telling the truth.

qa.q: Where did the teacher find Tarun's milk?
qa.a: The teacher found the full cup behind the plant pot.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Veer didn't believe him?
qa.a: He felt hurt and upset, crying because he was telling the truth.

qa.q: Why was the circle-time talk a good next step?
qa.a: It helped all the children see that lies make it hard to be believed later.

qa.q: How might Veer see Tarun after the milk lie?
qa.a: Veer didn't trust Tarun's words, remembering the earlier lie.

grounding: A teacher notes a five-year-old learning that a lie makes it hard to be believed later.

passage:
In their village near Kolhapur, Leela, five, knocked Aai's clay water pot off the step. It cracked.
When Aai came, Leela pointed at her brother. “Tejas did it.”
Tejas, eight, got a scolding. He looked at Leela, hurt, but said nothing.
That evening, Leela shouted that Tejas took her ribbon. Aai didn't listen. “Are you sure, Leela?”
Leela's lip wobbled. She whispered, “I broke the pot. Not Tejas.”
Aai hugged Tejas. Then she held Leela's hand. “Thank you for telling me. Now say sorry to your brother.”

qa.q: What did Leela knock off the step?
qa.a: She knocked Aai's clay water pot off the step.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when Aai didn't listen to her about the ribbon?
qa.a: She felt upset and guilty, her lip wobbling, because she knew she had lied before.

qa.q: What did Aai do that helped Leela learn?
qa.a: She thanked Leela for finally telling the truth and asked her to say sorry to her brother.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he was scolded for Leela's lie?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unfairly blamed, but stayed quiet.

grounding: A five-year-old sees how her lie stops her mother believing her, and tells the truth.

passage:
There was blue paint on the hallway carpet in the small London flat. "Wasn't me," said Emeka, hands behind his back. His hands were blue.
His sister Sofia sighed and scrubbed the carpet.
That afternoon, Emeka ran in shouting, "Sofia! The bath is overflowing!"
"Nice try," said Sofia, not looking up from her book.
Then water trickled under the bathroom door. Sofia ran. Together they turned off the tap.
Later, Emeka whispered, "The paint was me. Sorry." Sofia nodded. "Thanks for telling me now."

qa.q: What colour was the paint on the carpet?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he whispered that the paint was him?
qa.a: Emeka felt guilty and a bit worried, having seen that his lie made Sofia doubt him when it mattered.

qa.q: What could Sofia say to help Emeka keep telling the truth?
qa.a: Sofia could tell him honestly that she didn't believe him about the bath because of the paint, and that telling the truth helps her trust him again.

qa.q: How did Emeka's lie affect Sofia when he shouted about the bath?
qa.a: Sofia didn't believe him and ignored a real problem, because the paint lie had made his words harder to trust.

grounding: A child lies about spilled paint and then isn't believed when he tells the truth.

passage:
The week before Christmas, the kindergarten had a jar of gold star stickers. "One each," said Nazia Ma'am.
Later, Avni had two stars on her jumper.
"Avni, did you take an extra one?"
"No. Rudra gave it to me."
Rudra frowned. "I didn't."
Avni looked at the floor. Her cheeks went pink. The room was quiet.
"It was me," she said at last. "I wanted two."
Nazia Ma'am knelt down. "Thank you for telling the truth. Now, shall we put this one back for someone who hasn't got one?"

qa.q: How many stars did Nazia Ma'am say each child could have?
qa.a: One each.

qa.q: What does Avni's pink face suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Avni felt embarrassed and guilty once Rudra said he hadn't given her the star.

qa.q: Which choice by Nazia Ma'am helped, and why?
qa.a: Nazia Ma'am thanked Avni for the truth before fixing the problem, so Avni learned that owning up is safer than lying.

qa.q: How might Rudra feel when Avni first says he gave her the star?
qa.a: Rudra might feel confused and cross at being blamed for something he didn't do.

grounding: A preschooler lies about a sticker, sees the effect on a classmate and admits it.

passage:
I'm Madhav, Vaibhav's cousin. On Holi, someone threw a water balloon that hit Dadi's newspaper.
"Who did that?" Dadi asked.
Vaibhav said, "The monkey on the wall." We all looked. There was no monkey.
After that, when Vaibhav asked for more balloons, Dadi said, "Let's see. Maybe the monkey needs them." The other kids laughed. Vaibhav's ears went red.
Later I saw him go and sit next to Dadi. I couldn't hear everything, but I heard "sorry". Dadi gave him three balloons and a pat on the head.

qa.q: What did the water balloon hit?
qa.a: Dadi's newspaper.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when his ears went red?
qa.a: Vaibhav seemed embarrassed that everyone laughed and that Dadi no longer trusted what he said.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do the next time something like this happens?
qa.a: Vaibhav could simply say "It was me" straight away, so no one doubts him and the fun carries on. 🙂

qa.q: How does Madhav see what happened between Vaibhav and Dadi?
qa.a: Madhav can't hear it all but sees that Vaibhav went to say sorry and that Dadi forgave him warmly.

grounding: A cousin watches a child's Holi lie cost him trust until he apologises.

passage:
Monsoon Monday: Minakshi, five, broke her brother Farhan's clay pot and said, "The cat did it." Farhan believed her.
Wednesday: Farhan found clay on Minakshi's frock. He looked hurt. "You lied." He wouldn't let her play with his marbles.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when he found out about the lie?

grounding: Tracks a young child learning that a lie broke trust and honesty rebuilt it.

passage:
On the last hot day before the rains, the power went out and the fridge dripped. Gopika, six, was told not to eat the ice cream until dinner.
In the dark kitchen she ate a spoonful. Then three.
Her uncle Omkar found the melted tub. "Who ate it?"
"I don't know," Gopika said, licking her lip.
Omkar raised an eyebrow. Gopika's cheeks went hot. "Me. Sorry."
"Thank you for telling me," he said. "Now we share the rest before it melts."

qa.q: What was Gopika told not to eat?
qa.a: The ice cream, until dinner.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel when Omkar raised an eyebrow?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and guilty; her cheeks went hot.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that made telling the truth easier?
qa.a: He thanked her for being honest and shared the ice cream instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Gopika admits it?
qa.a: Omkar probably feels relieved and a bit amused that she told the truth.

grounding: Shows a young child trying a lie, then choosing honesty and seeing trust restored.

passage:
During the winter holidays, Vikas, five, drew on the wall of their Pune flat with a crayon. When his older cousin Gopika asked, he said, "Not me."
Gopika pointed at the purple crayon in his hand.
Vikas looked at it, then at her. "Maybe me."
"If you tell me the truth, I can trust you," she said.
He nodded slowly. "It was me. Can we wash it?"
They scrubbed together, giggling at the purple bubbles.

qa.q: What colour was the crayon in Vikas's hand?
qa.a: Purple.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt when Gopika pointed at the crayon?
qa.a: He likely felt caught and uneasy, then relieved after admitting it.

qa.q: How did Gopika help Vikas understand honesty?
qa.a: She linked truth to trust and helped him fix the wall together.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel after they scrub together?
qa.a: Gopika probably feels happy and closer to Vikas.

grounding: Shows a young child learning that honesty lets others trust him.

passage:
"Vijay, who broke the new diya?" Mummy held up the pieces. The house smelled of Diwali cleaning.
"The cat," said Vijay, five, looking at his feet.
"The cat was on the roof all morning."
Vijay's ears went red. "The cat… jumped down."
Mummy sat on the step. "If you tell me stories, how will I know when to believe you?"
Vijay's chin wobbled. "I did it. I was playing ball."
"Thank you for the truth." She handed him a broom. "Let's sweep it together, carefully."
His sister Jaya whispered, "I was scared too, once. Telling is better."

qa.q: What was Vijay doing when the diya broke?
qa.a: He was playing ball.

qa.q: What do Vijay's red ears suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and nervous, because he knew the cat story wasn't true.

qa.q: What went well in the way Mummy handled the lie?
qa.a: She calmly pointed out that the story didn't fit, explained how lies make it hard to believe someone, and thanked him when he told the truth.

qa.q: How does Jaya try to help Vijay?
qa.a: Jaya shares that she was scared once too, so Vijay feels less alone and knows that telling the truth is better.

grounding: Shows a young child trying out a lie, seeing it doesn't hold up, and learning that honesty keeps trust.
